Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Affective Expression: Crying, Crowding: Crowded places, Moral Violation: People misbehaving
  Threat: Door and Lock Checking: I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked, Threat in Silence: Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen, Watching Others: I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me
  Memory: Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened., Photographic Recall: Remembering what happened during the frightening event is just like looking at photographs of it in my mind., Overwhelm on Recall: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop

Vignette:
John, a 53-year-old married man from Oceania with an occupation as an airline pilot, has been grappling with symptoms of post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) following his experience of torture. Born and raised in the Pacific Islands, John had moved to America years ago for work, finding solace in the skies as a pilot for one of the major airlines. His life seemed steady until he was caught up in a series of events that led to him being subjected to severe physical and psychological abuse at the hands of individuals intent on silencing his activism efforts. The trauma John experienced was not just brutal but also deeply dehumanizing, leaving him with vivid memories that replay in stark detail. When he thinks about the frightening event, he can sometimes smell the damp earth and the acrid scent of sweat and fear that permeated the room where he was held captive. The memory feels like looking at a series of photographs, each one bringing back the exact sights and sounds of his ordeal. In the immediate aftermath of his release, John struggled to reconcile his life as an airline pilot with the horrific memories that haunted him. Crowded places became overwhelming triggers for him; the mere sight of people gathered in large numbers could send him into a state of panic. He began to avoid such environments altogether, often making excuses to bypass areas where crowds were likely to form. One particular incident stands out vividly. During a routine layover at an airport, he found himself surrounded by travelers rushing to catch their flights. The crowd's movement and the cacophony of voices triggered his trauma response so acutely that he had to excuse himself from work temporarily. This avoidance behavior began to affect his job performance, as he started missing flights and turning down assignments to avoid potential triggers. Moreover, John found himself hyper-vigilant, constantly monitoring for any signs of danger. He repeatedly checked that doors and windows were locked, even in the comfort of his own home. The silence was particularly unsettling; it often made him feel like something dangerous was about to happen. This hypervigilance extended beyond his personal life into his professional setting. During flights, he would watch other crew members closely for any signs that they might pose a threat, despite knowing rationally that such fears were unfounded. The emotional toll of these experiences became overwhelming. Simple acts like watching the news or seeing people misbehave could evoke intense feelings of distress and fear. He had come to believe that his safety was perpetually at risk, leading him to isolate himself from social interactions he once enjoyed. What frightened John most was the unpredictability of when his memories would return and how overwhelming they felt each time they surfaced. The emotional intensity was so profound that he often had to stop whatever he was doing until the memory passed. This led to significant disruptions in his daily life, affecting both his work as a pilot and his relationship with his wife. Despite his efforts to cope by avoiding certain situations and checking locks repeatedly, John realized that these behaviors were not helping him manage his symptoms but rather exacerbating them over time. He finally decided to seek help after a particularly distressing incident where he had to cancel an important flight due to his emotional state. The thought of potentially endangering passengers weighed heavily on him. In therapy, John hopes for relief from the constant fear and overwhelming memories that disrupt his life. He is most hopeful that with support, he can regain control over his emotions and daily functioning without having to avoid situations or people who trigger his trauma responses. His journey towards recovery begins as he works through these fears and seeks to rebuild a sense of safety in his world.
